faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my Trenton basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In Chambersburg rowhouses the signs gather in the rear basement kitchens, and the run almost always enters where a century of plumbing repairs passed through the same foundation wall. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: How is the price for a Trenton wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. A Hiltonia single with squirrels at one gable and a South Trenton rowhouse with a basement rat run price from different planets, and the separate lines for removal, sealing, and cleanup are how the owner sees that before deciding. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

Trenton.wildlife_intro:
Trenton is a river capital of brick rowhouses: Chambersburg's tight rowhouse blocks, Villa Park's twins, the larger homes of Hiltonia and the Cadwalader Park streets, and older housing down to the Delaware in South Trenton. Rats define the city's wildlife work, running the alleys, the old laterals, and the blocks behind the food corridors. Raccoons den in the porch roofs and the chimneys of vacant and occupied houses alike, squirrels work the park-side streets, and starlings and sparrows fill the vents and signs along the avenues.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. Trenton's rowhouses leak animals sideways through shared voids, so the inspection here maps the run of connected houses and the quote separates each owner's entries plainly.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Hamilton Township ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. In Mercerville's capes the morning running usually enters at a low eave reachable from a fence rail or a shed roof, and the chewed corner is rarely the only soft board on that run. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Hamilton Township garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. Creek-side Hamilton lots give groundhogs a banked den site within a few yards of the garden fence, and the burrow in the bank, not the fence, is where the trapping is set. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

Hamilton Township.wildlife_intro:
Hamilton is Mercer's big suburban township, a patchwork of named communities: Mercerville's postwar streets, Yardville's older village homes, Hamilton Square, Groveville, and the lakes and creek corridors between them. Crosswicks Creek and its tributaries keep green threads through the subdivisions. Squirrels and raccoons are the daily work in the capes and colonials, groundhogs dig along the creek banks and the bigger lots, skunks work the lawns, and bats take the quieter attics near the woods and water. It is classic suburbia at the age where every original soffit is suspect.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Hamilton's postwar soffits are failing on schedule across whole subdivisions, so the inspection here checks the full eave run and prices the replacement of the run, not a patch on the reported hole.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Princeton home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. A Jugtown colonial with a stone chimney raccoon family and a Riverside colonial with a decade of bat guano are both ordinary Princeton inspections, and their written quotes differ for reasons the line items make obvious. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Princeton attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. Princeton's big attics can hide a raccoon litter for a full season, and the thumping is often reported first by a guest in a third-floor bedroom rather than the owners below. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

Princeton.wildlife_intro:
Princeton's housing matches its reputation: substantial older homes in the western section, historic streets around the university, the Witherspoon-Jackson neighborhood's proud older blocks, and Jugtown's colonial-era houses, all under some of the state's heaviest canopy. Lake Carnegie and the D&R Canal frame the east and south. Squirrels and raccoons work the big attics and stone chimneys, bats hold colonies in the older homes near the canal and the institute woods, groundhogs and skunks take the deep lots, and the whole town is a short walk from open country in most directions.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Princeton's canopy bridges to more rooflines than almost anywhere in Mercer County, so limb distance and tree condition are reported with the sealing plan on every job.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Ewing Township lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. Ewing's river-side lawns grow grubs in rich soil, and the skunk cone-holing often maps the damp low corner of the yard where the larvae concentrate. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

faqs.q: I can hear baby animals in my Ewing Township wall — can you just seal the hole?
faqs.a: Not yet, and any company offering to should worry you. Sealing a mother out with a litter inside converts a removal into dead animals in the wall. A Ewing chimney litter is usually heard as chirping behind the fireplace wall in April, and the camera check comes before any cap conversation, every time. We locate the litter first, then time the work so the family leaves or is taken out together — one-way exits sized for the species, or hands-on removal where the young cannot climb. The hole gets sealed the same visit the last animal is confirmed out, not before.

Ewing Township.wildlife_intro:
Ewing wraps around Trenton's northwest side: West Trenton's older river streets, postwar subdivisions through the township's middle, the College of New Jersey's green campus, and the Delaware River and Scudder Falls at the western edge. The housing is mostly mid-century capes, ranches, and colonials now under mature trees. Squirrels and raccoons lead the calls, groundhogs work the river-side and field-edge lots, rats appear around the older corridors near the city line, and bats pick the quieter attics near the river woods.

Garages and sheds are the soft underbelly of a property. A garage door that stops a quarter-inch high, a shed set straight on soil, stored birdseed and grass seed in open bags — raccoons, rats, skunks, and opossums all read that as an invitation. Proofing means door sweeps and corner seals on the garage, hardware-cloth skirts on the shed, and feed and seed moved into lidded metal bins. Many house infestations turn out to start in the garage and commute through a shared attic or a breezeway, so the outbuildings get inspected with the house, every time. Ewing's garages and breezeways are the commuting route on many of these lots, so the outbuilding seals are quoted with the house work instead of discovered during it.

faqs.q: Moles are tearing up my Lawrence Township yard — how are they handled?
faqs.a: By trapping the active runs, not by poison peanuts or vibrating stakes, which mostly rearrange the damage. Surface ridges are feeding tunnels; the deep runs along edges and foundations are the travel lanes where traps belong. Lawrence's big, watered backyards are mole habitat by design, and the ridging here tends to follow the property's drainage swale from the wet end to the garden. Eastern moles work most New Jersey lawns, and the star-nosed mole turns up in wetter ground. Expect a few visits spaced out — mole work is verified by fresh ridging stopping, not by a single day's catch.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Lawrence Township attic actually a fire risk?
faqs.a: They can be. Squirrels gnaw constantly to wear their teeth, and wiring, PVC, and stored paper are all fair game; chewed conductors in a hot attic are a genuine hazard, not a sales line. In Lawrenceville's oldest attics the wiring runs through two centuries of alterations, and gnawed runs are photographed and flagged because the next stop for that information is the owner's electrician, not a shrug. Once the squirrels are out and the entries are meshed, we flag any chewed wiring we saw so an electrician can judge it — that check is part of why a squirrel job should never end at just closing the hole.

Lawrence Township.wildlife_intro:
Lawrence sits between Trenton and Princeton and carries both influences: the historic village of Lawrenceville on Main Street, the Route 1 corridor's commercial sprawl with subdivisions behind it, Colonial Lake, and farm and corporate-campus open space holding the township's green frame. Housing runs from 1700s village homes to postwar Slackwood streets to newer colonials. Squirrels and raccoons work the village and the older subdivisions, groundhogs take the field edges, moles ridge the corporate-lawn-quality yards, and bats settle near the lake and the Shabakunk corridors.

Newer houses are not exempt — they just fail differently. Vinyl soffits flex and pop at the corners, roof-to-wall joints on additions open as materials settle, and bathroom vents often end in cheap plastic covers that starlings and squirrels push through in a season. Builders leave gaps around garage door corners and utility lines that rats and mice find within the first year. The work on a newer home is detail work: metal where plastic failed, backer rod and sealant at settling joints, and screens behind every vent cover rather than trust in the cover alone. Lawrence mixes colonial-era construction with subdivisions built last decade, and the inspection here runs two checklists, one for each era's characteristic gaps.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Hightstown attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. The lake-side attics hold Hightstown's summer colonies, and callers in June get the survey, the documentation, and a dated place in the August window, because a maternity roost handled early is a small job and handled late is not. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

faqs.q: What makes one Hightstown wildlife job cost more than another?
faqs.a: Access, animal count, and aftermath. A steep roof, a maternity litter that has to be handled as a family, or insulation contaminated wall-to-wall all add time and material. Hightstown's range is set by its housing: a twin with one squirrel entry on one end, and a three-story Victorian with a bat colony and a failed chimney crown on the other. The inspection sorts your house into one of those buckets and the written quote shows exactly which items drive the number.

Hightstown.wildlife_intro:
Hightstown is a small, complete borough: a historic Main Street, Peddie Lake at its center, Rocky Brook running through, and tight older neighborhoods of Victorians, colonials, and twins that East Windsor's subdivisions wrap around. The lake and brook put habitat in the middle of town. Raccoons den in the older chimneys within a block of the water, bats hold the tall attics on the side streets, squirrels work the street trees into the eaves, and groundhogs dig the lots that back onto the brook and the borough's remaining open ground.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Hightstown's brick chimneys are old, tall, and mostly uncapped, and fitting them properly is the single highest-value job in the borough.
